name: Acute Pyelonephritis

pathogens.why: Pyelonephritis pathogens largely mirror uncomplicated UTI but with greater clinical consequence of undertreatment, since ascending infection from the same uropathogens can progress to bacteremia and sepsis.

investigations.why: Confirms organism and susceptibility, essential for targeted therapy and de-escalation.
Pyelonephritis carries meaningful bacteremia risk; positive cultures confirm systemic involvement and guide duration.

investigations.test: Renal ultrasound or CT (if no improvement in 48-72 hours)
investigations.why: Evaluates for obstruction or abscess if the patient fails to improve on appropriate therapy.

reason: indicates upper urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis). This requires antibiotics with reliable renal tissue penetration,
and given hemodynamic instability, urgent IV therapy and evaluation for urosepsis
with outpatient oral therapy appropriate in hemodynamically stable, tolerating patients

clinicalPearls: Fever is the principal feature distinguishing pyelonephritis from simple cystitis; presence of fever, back/flank pain, rigors, nausea or vomiting signals infection that has extended beyond the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1086-1090, 1133).

Severity spans a wide spectrum: mild disease may present only with low-grade fever with or without costovertebral angle pain, whereas severe disease manifests with high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain; onset is generally acute and may or may not be preceded by cystitis symptoms (Harrison 22e p.1090).
Pyelonephritis represents tissue-invasive disease and patients are often systemically ill, so the threat of progression to bacteremia and urosepsis is real (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137, 1329).

In a woman presenting with at least one localizing urinary symptom (dysuria, frequency, hematuria, or back pain) and no complicating factors, the combined probability of acute cystitis or pyelonephritis is about 50% (Harrison 22e p.1133).

Men with febrile UTI should undergo upper-tract imaging (CT or ultrasound) if not done previously, to evaluate for urinary tract abnormality or obstruction, and elevated PSA with enlarged prostate/seminal vesicles suggests prostatic involvement (Harrison 22e p.1132).

Pregnant patients are at unusually high risk of developing pyelonephritis, which can adversely affect pregnancy outcome (preterm delivery, low birth weight); this underlies routine prenatal screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria (Harrison 22e p.1086, 1329).
harrison.pathophysiology: Pyelonephritis usually develops as an ascending infection: uropathogens move from the urethra to the bladder and then continue up the ureter to the renal parenchyma, which is the route for most renal parenchymal infection. Its microbiology therefore mirrors that of acute cystitis. A minority arises hematogenously (<2% of UTIs overall), typically with relatively virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Salmonella; isolation of either from urine should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia, and hematogenous seeding can produce focal renal abscesses. Anatomic factors causing urinary obstruction or retention (congenital anomalies, cystocele, pelvic-organ prolapse, neurogenic bladder, benign prostatic hypertrophy) impede the protective flushing action of micturition and predispose to renal involvement. A foreign body such as a stone or catheter provides an inert surface for colonization (Harrison 22e p.1088, 1130-1131).
additionalDifferentials: Acute prostatitis in men presenting with febrile UTI (Harrison 22e p.1137)
Complicated UTI (fever in a patient with structural/functional urinary abnormality, immunocompromise, or instrumentation) (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Sexually transmitted infection mimicking UTI, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis cervicitis/urethritis (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Renal/ureteral calculus with obstruction (renal colic) presenting with flank pain and pyuria (Harrison 22e p.2493)
infectionMimics: Cervicitis or urethritis due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Vaginitis (Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis) or herpetic urethritis causing dysuria (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
nonInfectiousMimics: Renal/ureteral stone with proximal obstruction, which may present exactly as acute pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2493)
Interstitial cystitis or noninfectious vulvovaginal irritation causing dysuria (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Sloughed renal papilla or blood clot causing ureteral obstruction without infection (Harrison 22e p.2493)
Musculoskeletal flank/back pain, herpes zoster, abdominal aortic aneurysm, duodenal ulcer (differential for flank pain) (Harrison 22e p.2493)
additionalInvestigations: Upper-tract imaging (CT or renal ultrasound) to evaluate for obstruction, abscess, or anatomic abnormality, especially in men, in patients not responding within 72 hours, or when complicated infection is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1132, 1137)

Urine dipstick (nitrite, leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis as point-of-care tests; note nitrites detect only Enterobacterales and may be falsely negative with non-Enterobacterales organisms (Harrison 22e p.1134-1135)
Imaging for gas in renal/perinephric tissues when emphysematous pyelonephritis is suspected in a diabetic patient (Harrison 22e p.1090)
redFlags: Acute papillary necrosis with sloughed papillae obstructing the ureter, producing obstructive uropathy that requires intervention to relieve obstruction and preserve renal function (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137)
UTI in the setting of ureteral obstruction is a medical emergency requiring immediate restoration of drainage by ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy (Harrison 22e p.2493)

Emphysematous pyelonephritis: gas production in renal and perinephric tissues, occurring almost exclusively in patients with poorly controlled diabetes; a particularly severe form (Harrison 22e p.1090)
Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibacterial therapy should raise suspicion for intraparenchymal, perinephric, or renal cortical abscess (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137)
Failure of clinical response within 72 hours warrants evaluation for an uncontrolled source of infection (Harrison 22e p.1137)
Persistently elevated/increasing fever, flank pain, and rising neutrophil counts should prompt evaluation for intrarenal/perinephric abscess and/or obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1329)
Bilateral papillary necrosis may present first as a rapid rise in serum creatinine (Harrison 22e p.1090)
harrison.prognosis: Most pyelonephritis treated effectively resolves, though fever may take 5-7 days to clear completely even with appropriate therapy. Renal parenchymal damage and loss of renal function are uncommon and occur primarily in association with urinary obstruction (preexisting, or, rarely, de novo in diabetic patients with papillary necrosis). Chronic bacterial pyelonephritis is rarely a cause of chronic renal failure because it seldom affects both kidneys. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis arises from chronic obstruction (often staghorn calculus) plus chronic infection causing suppurative destruction of renal tissue and frequently requires nephrectomy (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137, 1329, 2493).
pitfalls: Treating presumed UTI when the true cause is an STI (e.g., C. trachomatis); vaginal discharge should prompt STI consideration since symptoms alone do not reliably distinguish them (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134).

Stopping the workup at an abnormal urinalysis in a catheterized or febrile patient: pyuria and bacteriuria are expected with catheterization and do not by themselves establish UTI as the cause of fever (Harrison 22e p.1133-1135).
Mistaking an obstructing stone with proximal infection for uncomplicated pyelonephritis and missing the need for emergent drainage (Harrison 22e p.2493).
Misattributing xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis to renal malignancy because its mass effect can mimic tumor (Harrison 22e p.1090).
Delayed/withheld antimicrobial therapy in true UTI carries a small increased risk of progression to pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1136).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison describes a clinical spectrum rather than a formal score: mild pyelonephritis (low-grade fever, with or without lower back or costovertebral angle pain) versus severe pyelonephritis (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain). Distinct severe/complicated entities include emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas-forming, almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetes), xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (chronic obstruction plus infection causing suppurative renal destruction), and pyelonephritis complicated by papillary necrosis with obstruction or by intrarenal/perinephric abscess. Acute pyelonephritis is one of the systemic UTI presentations that may be grouped as urosepsis or febrile UTI, with or without bacteremia (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1329).
